name: Rally / CA Agile Central (Broadcom)
summary: Rally (formerly CA Agile Central, now ValueOps Rally by Broadcom) is the long-tenured enterprise SAFe tool that predates most modern Git-aware trackers. It treats source control as a first-class read-only stream of two object types: Changesets (Rally's name for VCS commits) and Pull Requests, both modelled as native Rally objects associated to User Stories, Defects, Defect Suites, Test Cases, and Tasks. The VCS connector is policy-based and one-way (Git -> Rally, never the reverse), parsing FormattedIDs (US1234, DE5678) from commit messages or PR titles to wire artefacts together. Where Rally is genuinely strong is on the quality side: Test Cases are first-class artefacts with bi-directional story linkage and a native Test Cases tab on every story, and Release is a native object distinct from Iteration. Where Rally is weak is on modern VCS surfacing: the card face shows none of this — all PR, Changeset, Build, and Test data lives behind the Connections tab in the work item detail editor, and the Rally Bot GitHub App explicitly does not process draft pull requests. The result is an enterprise tool with the data model to support rich traceability but a card-and-board UI vocabulary frozen around 2014.
card_surface: Effectively nothing VCS-related on the card face by default. Rally cards on Team Boards, Kanban Boards, and the Custom Board app always show ID (formatted as US1234 / DE5678), Name, and Owner, and administrators can add up to roughly 10 additional fields via 'Show Fields' / 'Show on Cards' configuration. The field list is the standard artefact field set — Plan Estimate, Schedule State, Flow State, Iteration, Release, Tags, Blocked (with a stop-sign icon), Ready, Expedite — none of which are PR-derived. There is no native 'Pull Requests' badge, no 'Changesets' counter, no PR status pill, no CI build glyph, and no branch name on the standard card. A 'Blocked' stop-sign and a 'Ready' tick are the only state icons in the default vocabulary. The only Git-adjacent surfacing on a card requires the Custom Board app with a custom renderer (CardBoardCardRenderer subclass) — engineering teams can override the renderer to read the Changesets or PullRequests collection counts and paint custom badges, but this is a developer-only escape hatch, not an out-of-the-box feature. Empty state is the default state — for most Rally users, cards never show VCS information at all. [uncertain] Some workspaces with Rally Anywhere / ValueOps modern UI experiments may have added small Connections counters to cards, but this is not documented in mainline Rally help.
detail_panel: Surfaced via the Connections collection in the work item detail editor — a set of typed tabs beneath the main story fields. Tab list (administrator-controlled per workspace): Tasks, Test Cases, Test Sets, Defects, Discussions, Revision History, Dependencies, Predecessors/Successors, and the VCS-specific tabs Changesets, Pull Requests, and Builds. Each tab opens an inline grid. The Changesets tab shows commit SHA (linked back to GitHub/Bitbucket/TFS), commit message (one-line), author, timestamp, and the SCMRepository name; the row click-throughs go to the source tool. The Pull Requests tab shows PR external ID/number, PR title, repository, source -> target branch (when populated), state (Open / Merged — Closed/Declined typically appears as 'Closed'), and a click-through URL. Author appears as a field but reviewer state, approval counts, requested reviewers, and CI checks-on-PR are NOT first-class — they live one click away in the source tool. The Builds tab (driven by the Jenkins / Build Connector) shows Build Number, BuildDefinition name, Status (SUCCESS / FAILURE / INCOMPLETE / NO_BUILDS), Duration, and start timestamp, with the SCM Changesets that fed the build listed beneath. There is no unified 'Development' panel like Jira's — each Connections type renders independently, in its own tab, with grid-style rows rather than a synthesized timeline. Branch name is not stored as a discrete field; it appears only as parsed text in commit messages or PR data.
state_coupling: Yes, and unusually first-class — Rally was one of the earliest enterprise trackers to support commit-driven state transitions, and the VCS connector ships with a dedicated state-update syntax. The default convention parses the commit message or PR body for the FormattedID followed by a target Schedule State or Defect State: 'US1234 In-Progress', 'US1234 Completed', 'DE5678 Fixed'. When the connector sees a match, it writes the ScheduleState (for User Stories), State (for Defects, Tasks, Defect Suites), or Flow State directly to the artefact. The GitHub-specific 'Rally Bot' app extends this with PR-body commands — '/completes US1234' in the merged PR body transitions the story Flow State to Complete, configurable via the mergeOnPRBody setting. Trigger granularity: per-workspace connector configuration with per-repository policy filtering — a workspace admin can decide that only the 'main' branch counts for state changes, that only merged (not opened) PRs trigger transitions, and which Schedule State target value applies. Triggers natively supported: commit pushed (with state syntax in message), pull request opened, pull request merged. Pull request closed/declined is captured as state on the PR object but does NOT typically trigger a story state regression. The coupling is opt-in per workspace and per artefact-state-target — not on by default — and is well-known as one of Rally's enterprise differentiators for shops where 'merge to main = story Done' is a hard policy.
draft_vs_ready_state: Effectively unsupported. The Rally Bot GitHub App Integration documentation states explicitly that connections do not work on draft pull requests — the app simply does not process draft PRs into Rally artefacts until they are marked Ready for Review. The older policy-based VCS Connector for GitHub will ingest a draft PR if the FormattedID is present (since it polls the GitHub API for all open PRs) but does not store a discrete 'isDraft' field on the Rally Pull Request object — the PR appears in the Pull Requests tab with state 'Open' indistinguishable from a ready-for-review PR. Third-party adapters (ConnectALL, OpsHub) can map GitHub's draft boolean to a custom Rally field or to a specific ScheduleState target via mapping rules, but this is a customer-configured workaround, not a native capability. Net effect for a developer scanning Rally: a draft PR either does not appear in Rally at all (Rally Bot path) or appears as a regular Open PR (legacy connector path) — there is no card-face or panel-level affordance to distinguish work-in-progress drafts from review-ready PRs. This is a meaningful gap relative to GitHub Projects v2 or Linear, both of which surface draft state as a distinct icon.
review_state: Not surfaced at all. The Rally Pull Request object captures the PR's top-level state (Open, Merged, Closed) and its external URL, but reviewer approval counts, blocking reviews, requested reviewers, review comments, and reviewer avatars are NOT stored as first-class fields on the Rally PR record. The Pull Requests tab in the Connections collection shows the PR row with author and state — to inspect reviewer state, a developer or RTE must click the URL through to GitHub/Bitbucket/Azure DevOps. The Rally Bot GitHub App does publish back to GitHub's Checks API with a pass/fail check called 'Rally + GitHub Integration' that validates artefact-state alignment between the PR and the linked story, but this is a Rally-imposed gate on the GitHub side rather than a Rally-side surfacing of GitHub's review state. No card-face approval count, no '2/2 approved' pill, no reviewer avatars. For James-style 'I am the reviewer on this PR' personas, Rally provides zero direct signal — they would rely entirely on the GitHub/Bitbucket UI for review queue management.
dod_checklist: Not first-class. Rally has no built-in Definition of Done checklist field, no native checklist primitive, and no Marketplace ecosystem of checklist apps comparable to Jira's Smart Checklist or Checklists for Jira. Teams implement DoD via three workaround patterns: (1) Tasks on the story used as DoD items — each story owns a Tasks collection where teams add 'Code reviewed', 'Tests written', 'Demo recorded' as discrete Task records with Owner and Actuals; the Tasks count and completion percentage are exposed on the story and can be added to card layout, giving a crude DoD progress indicator. (2) Acceptance Criteria text field — a rich-text field on User Story where DoD bullets are written as markdown/HTML; no structured completion tracking, purely descriptive. (3) Custom fields — workspace admins can add a 'Definition of Done' custom field (multi-select or rich-text) and use it as a soft gate. None of these are templated per issue type, none of them block Schedule State transitions, and none of them aggregate to a card-face DoD pill. The Tasks-as-DoD approach is the most common but has the side effect that DoD items pollute the Tasks count alongside real engineering tasks, which is a known antipattern. The honest summary: Rally treats DoD as a process convention enforced by the Scrum Master, not as a tracked data field.
test_linkage: First-class and one of Rally's genuine strengths. Test Case is a native Rally artefact type (not an app, not a marketplace add-on) with its own FormattedID prefix (TC), its own detail page, and its own collection grid. A User Story has a native Test Cases tab in the Connections collection where Test Cases are added inline ('Add New' button creates a TC scoped to the story, 'Add Existing' links a TC from elsewhere), and the linkage is bi-directional — opening a Test Case shows the linked Work Product (story or defect) as a native field. Test Cases have their own first-class fields: Method (Manual / Automated), Type (Acceptance / Functional / Regression / Performance / Usability), Priority, Risk, Validation Inputs, Validation Expected Result, Pre-Conditions, Post-Conditions. Test Sets group Test Cases for a test run. Test Case Results record per-execution outcomes (Pass / Fail / Blocked / Inconclusive / Error) with Build, Tester, Date, Tested By, Notes. On the User Story detail page, 'Test Case Status' is a derived rollup showing the most recent result per linked TC, and a 'Last Verdict' field can be exposed on the card. A User Story can be flagged 'complete only when all linked Test Cases pass' as a workspace policy. CI test results (from Jenkins / Bamboo / GitHub Actions) flow into the separate Build object, not into Test Case Results — automated unit/integration test counts are stored as fields on the Build (Test Status, Number Tests, Number Failures, Number Errors, Number Passing, Number Skipped, Number Not Hung). The split is deliberate: Test Cases = human/functional/acceptance tests, Builds = CI-driven unit/integration tests. The two are NOT unified on the card face or in a single 'Tests' panel; a developer or RTE has to know which collection to open. Card-face surfacing: 'Last Verdict' can be added to card layout but is text-only ('Pass'/'Fail'), not a coloured pill, and no card-face coverage badge exists out of the box.
cicd_status: Surfaced via the Build object — a first-class Rally artefact type populated by build connectors (Rally Build Connector for Jenkins, Bamboo plug-in, ConnectALL adapters for CircleCI / GitHub Actions / Azure Pipelines / GitLab CI). Each Build object holds BuildDefinition (the Jenkins job, persisted as its own Rally object), Number, Status (SUCCESS / FAILURE / INCOMPLETE / NO_BUILDS / UNKNOWN), Duration, Start, URI (link back to Jenkins console), and the SCM Changesets that fed the build. The Connector pulls SCM ChangeSet information from Jenkins, matches commits to artefacts via FormattedID parsing, and writes a Build relationship onto each affected story or defect. Visual treatment: in the Connections > Builds tab, each row shows a coloured status text (green SUCCESS, red FAILURE) with no icon, no inline progress indicator, no individual check names — only the aggregate per-build verdict. The Build Status page (a separate top-level Tracking page) lists builds across the workspace with filterable status, but is not card-integrated. On the card face, no CI status appears by default — even adding 'Last Build Status' as a custom field is not natively supported; teams use the Build Action Board community app (RallyCommunity/BuildActionBoard) or a custom dashboard chart for visibility. A failing CI run does not auto-create a story-level risk signal or block a Schedule State transition — surfacing it as an attention signal requires a custom rule built on the Rally WSAPI or a dashboard chart. Individual check names (e.g. 'lint', 'unit-tests', 'security-scan') are NOT preserved — Rally stores only the build-level verdict.
release_tagging: Release is a native first-class Rally object — one of Rally's older and more deeply integrated data primitives, dating to the original CA Agile Central data model. Release has its own fields (Name, Theme, Release Start Date, Release Date, Plan Estimate Capacity, Notes) and its own Release Tracking page that aggregates child stories, defects, and portfolio items. A User Story has a Release field (single-valued — a story belongs to one Release, unlike Jira's multi-valued Fix Version) and a separate Iteration field (a story belongs to one Iteration scoped within a Release). On the card face, Release and Iteration can both be added via 'Show on Cards' and render as text labels (e.g. 'Release: 2026.Q2' or 'PI-26.2'). Portfolio Items (Feature, Capability, Epic, Initiative, Theme — the configurable SAFe hierarchy) can also be assigned to a Release, and Release status rolls up via the Release Tracking page showing total stories, accepted count, defect count, and burndown. Git tags from GitHub/Bitbucket are NOT automatically mapped to Release objects — they appear as separate fields on the Changeset object (Commit.Branch, Commit.Tag if populated) but do not auto-create or auto-assign Rally Release records. A story can only belong to one Release at a time, which means backport scenarios require either creating duplicate stories or using a custom multi-select 'Additional Releases' custom field — a known Rally limitation that Jira's multi-Fix-Version model handles more gracefully. Release labels are configurable per workspace (a workspace can rename 'Release' to 'PI' or 'Train Increment') via the configurable-labels feature.
aggregation: Strong at the Schedule State / Plan Estimate level, absent at the VCS / PR / Build level. Portfolio Items (Feature, Capability, Epic, Initiative) automatically aggregate Schedule State counts, accepted story points, and percentage-complete from child stories via Rally's built-in rollup engine — a Feature card on the Portfolio Item page shows 'X of Y stories accepted', total story points, and a coloured status dot driven by an algorithm that weighs story count, story points, dates accepted, and planned start/end. This rollup is automatic, real-time, and does not require Automation rules. However, Pull Request count, Changeset count, Build status, and Test Case pass rate do NOT roll up from child stories to the parent Feature or Epic. A Feature with 5 child stories — even if all 5 have merged PRs — will show empty Pull Requests and Changesets tabs on the Feature itself (since developers reference story IDs in commits, not feature IDs). The native gap is real: there is no '3 of 5 stories have merged PRs' indicator on a Feature card, no aggregate CI verdict at the Feature level, no aggregated test coverage rollup at the Portfolio Item level. Workarounds include custom Lookback API charts on dashboards, the Traceability Matrix community app (RallyApps/TraceabilityMatrix), and the BuildTraceability community app — all of which compute the rollup externally and render it as a separate chart, not as a card-face indicator. [uncertain] Newer ValueOps Insights and ValueOps Connect surfaces may aggregate this at the value stream level, but the core Rally board cards do not.
environment_deployment_target: Supported via the separate Continuous Delivery Director (CDD) plug-in and the Build object, but not directly surfaced on Rally cards. CDD is Broadcom's release-orchestration product that integrates with Rally to import work items into release content, track which stories are included in which deployment, and write back deployment status. When CDD or Jenkins push a deployment event, the connector can update a custom 'Deployed To' field on the story or write a discrete Deployment Action record — but Deployment is NOT a first-class Rally object like Changeset or Pull Request, and there is no native Environment field on the User Story. The Build object can hold environment context (via Build.Tags or BuildDefinition naming conventions like 'deploy-prod', 'deploy-staging') but it is convention-driven, not schema-enforced. On the card face: no deployment badge, no environment pill, no 'In Staging / In Prod' indicator. In the detail panel: deployment status can be added as a custom field for workspaces that have set up the CDD plug-in, but the standard out-of-the-box Rally workspace shows no deployment signal at all. Compared to Jira's Deployments row, Azure DevOps Environments, or Linear's release pipeline, Rally's deployment surfacing is markedly weaker — it is a connector-driven write into custom fields rather than a typed, schema-aware deployment timeline. RTEs and PMs tracking 'which feature is in production' rely on the Release object's release-status field plus CDD's pipeline view, not on the Rally card itself.
traceability_completeness: Rich underlying data model, no synthesized card-face indicator. Rally has more raw traceability primitives than most competitors — Story has Tasks, Test Cases (with verdicts), Defects, Discussions, Changesets, Pull Requests, Builds, Predecessors/Successors, Dependencies, and Portfolio Item parent — all stored as typed collections on a single artefact. This means the data exists to compute a composite '✓ code · ✓ tests · ✓ DoD · ✓ deploy' indicator. But Rally does NOT synthesize these into a single visual signal on the card or detail page. The Traceability Matrix is exposed as a separate community app (RallyApps/TraceabilityMatrix) that renders a grid view (story rows x linkage columns), the BuildTraceability app shows artefacts per build, and dashboard charts can compute composite readiness percentages via the Lookback API — but none of these appear as a card-face progress ring or icon strip. Custom approaches include a workspace-defined 'Ready for Release' boolean populated by WSAPI scripts when (PR merged + all Test Cases pass + Tasks 100% complete) hits, surfaced as a card field — but this is shop-built infrastructure, not a Rally feature. Rally Insights (ValueOps Insights) and the Rally Program Dashboard offer aggregated traceability KPIs at the program/portfolio level (test coverage %, build pass rate, deployment frequency), but these are dashboard tiles, not card indicators. The pattern of a single composite traceability dot on a story card is a clear gap — and given the richness of Rally's underlying data, it is one of the higher-value design patterns an EAP prototype could fill.
design_pattern: Tabbed Connections collection in the detail editor; nothing on the card face by default. Rally's design vocabulary is rooted in pre-2015 enterprise UI conventions: data lives in grids, relationships live in named collection tabs, and the card is a compact summary with text-only fields. The Connections collection is a tab strip (Tasks | Test Cases | Defects | Changesets | Pull Requests | Builds | Discussions | Revision History | Dependencies) where each tab opens a flat grid of related rows. State is encoded as text and small monochrome icons in the grid — Status column shows 'Open' / 'Merged' as plain text; Build status shows 'SUCCESS' / 'FAILURE' coloured green/red; Test Case Last Verdict shows 'Pass' / 'Fail'. No status pills, no icon strip, no badges. The pattern is consistent across artefact types — every Story, Defect, Defect Suite, Task, and Test Case has the same Connections collection structure (with type-appropriate tabs hidden where N/A). Empty state is empty tabs — a tab with no rows simply shows 'No Items' text. Compared to Jira's compact counter-icon strip on the card face, Linear's single-colour pill compression, or Targetprocess's full block visualisation, Rally is the most data-rich but visually least expressive: the information is all there if you know to open the right tab, but nothing surfaces at glance distance. This is a coherent choice for an enterprise audience where 'I will open the detail editor to inspect' is the assumed workflow, but it fails badly against the modern bar set by Linear, Shortcut, and GitHub Projects. Custom Board apps can override the renderer to paint badges from the Connections data, but this requires JavaScript SDK development per workspace.
